name: Pxxl
tagline: A managed platform for deploying web apps, static sites and files with a URL you can hand to someone.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely write you a mini PaaS: a CLI that tars a folder, ships it to a box, builds a Docker image and points Caddy at a subdomain. What it cannot write is the box, the bandwidth, the wildcard TLS that never expires, the machine that stays up while you sleep, or the part where a deploy still works six months after you forgot how any of it fits together. Hosting is a product where the code is the cheap half. You will end up renting a server anyway, which means you replaced a bill with a bill plus a pager. Build it if you want to learn Docker plumbing, not if you want your side project to stay online.
coreLoopDIY: A one-command deploy script that pushes a folder to your own VPS, builds it in Docker, and serves it on a wildcard subdomain with automatic TLS.
requirements: A VPS you pay for and patch yourself
A domain with a wildcard DNS record pointing at it
Docker and Caddy on the host
SSH keys and a willingness to debug builds over SSH at midnight
whatYouLose: Someone else being on call when the host reboots or the disk fills
Automatic TLS renewal that you never have to think about
Build environments for multiple runtimes that already work
Bandwidth and CDN that survive a link getting shared widely
A dashboard, logs and rollbacks that exist without you writing them
moatNotes: Managed hosting is mostly an uptime promise. Code cannot make that promise on your behalf.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is being your own sysadmin for the rest of the project's life. A deploy CLI is a fun weekend, but the value of hosting shows up in the boring months after: certificates renewing, the container restarting after an OOM, the build cache not rotting, the URL still resolving when someone clicks it a year later. Paying a platform converts an ongoing operational obligation into a line item, and for anything with real users that trade is almost always correct.
notes: The deploy script is a weekend; the uptime is not. The moat is owned infrastructure plus the fact that nobody wants to be paged for their own hobby project.
prompt:
Build a minimal self-hosted deploy platform for one person, in an empty folder.

Stack, no alternatives:
- Host target: a single Ubuntu 24.04 VPS I already own, with Docker and Caddy installed by your setup script.
- CLI: Node 20, plain JavaScript, ESM, no TypeScript, no framework. Entry point bin/deploy.js.
- Routing and TLS: Caddy with on-demand TLS and a wildcard DNS record for *.apps.example.com.
- Transport: ssh and rsync over an existing key. No agent, no daemon on the host beyond Docker and Caddy.

What it must do:
1. `deploy init` writes a .deployrc in the current project: app name, port, build type (static or dockerfile).
2. `deploy up` rsyncs the project to /srv/apps/NAME on the host, ignoring node_modules and .git.
3. For static builds, run the configured build command locally, ship only the output dir, and serve it with a generated Caddy file_server block.
4. For dockerfile builds, build the image on the host, run it with a restart policy of unless-stopped, and reverse_proxy NAME.apps.example.com to its container port.
5. Blue/green: start the new container, health check GET / until 200 with a 30 second timeout, then swap the Caddy upstream and stop the old container. On failure, leave the old one running and exit nonzero.
6. `deploy logs` tails docker logs. `deploy rollback` swaps back to the previous image tag. `deploy rm` deletes app, container, files and Caddy block.
7. Keep the last 3 image tags per app, prune the rest.
8. A single JSON state file at /srv/apps/state.json is the source of truth. Regenerate the Caddy config from it and reload Caddy, never hand-edit.

Rules:
- Secrets: host, user and domain come from .env, with .env.example committed. No secrets in the repo.
- No accounts, no web dashboard, no telemetry, no database.
- Idempotent: running `deploy up` twice in a row must be safe.
- Include scripts/bootstrap.sh that installs Docker and Caddy on a fresh VPS and creates /srv/apps.
- README with the exact DNS records needed and a one-app worked example.

Out of scope: multi-user auth, build queues, custom domains per app beyond a CNAME note in the README, managed databases, autoscaling.
